Neonatal false killer whales (Pseudorca crassidens) are born at a relatively large size, with a total length at birth of approximately 174 centimeters [Lb = approximately 174 centimeters]. This substantial neonatal length is typical among large delphinids and is thought to confer advantages in thermoregulation and predator avoidance for the newborn calf during its critical first weeks of life. Field observations of wild stocks in Hawaiian waters suggest that births can occur year-round, although a peak in calving may align with warmer sea surface temperatures. The gestation period supporting this substantial investment in offspring size is notably extended; anatomical and observational records indicate that pregnancy lasts approximately 451 days [tg = approximately 451 days] at a core maternal body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This prolonged gestation, comparable to that of other large-bodied odontocetes, allows for substantial foetal development and contributes to the precocial nature of the newborn.

Following birth, the nursing calf remains almost entirely dependent on its mother's extremely lipid-rich milk for sustenance. The time since birth at weaning, marking the transition to nutritional independence, has been estimated at about 730 days [tx = about 730 days] based on observational studies of mother-calf pairs, with this duration measured at a standard body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This protracted period of maternal investment, often exceeding two years, is one of the longest documented among delphinids and reflects the complex social learning required for successful foraging on large pelagic fish and squid. During this extended nursing phase, the calf grows steadily, learning fundamental hunting techniques and social behaviors from its mother and other pod members. The gradual process of weaning is rarely abrupt and may involve a progressive reduction in nursing frequency over many months, during which the juvenile begins to ingest solid food with increasing proficiency before achieving complete milk independence.

The developmental trajectory of Pseudorca crassidens reveals pronounced sexual dimorphism in both size and the timing of life history events. Females attain sexual maturity considerably earlier than males; the time since birth at puberty for females is recorded as 3468 days [tp = 3468 days] under typical warm-bodied conditions of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], equivalent to approximately 9.5 years of age. In contrast, the time since birth at puberty for males is substantially longer, measured at approximately 6756 days [tp = approximately 6756 days] at the same core temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], representing roughly 18.5 years. This protracted male maturation period is among the most extreme reported for any cetacean species and is likely linked to the highly polygynous or promiscuous mating system, where males must achieve considerable body size and social standing to compete effectively for reproductive opportunities.

Adult body size in false killer whales is markedly sexually dimorphic, reflecting the disparate energetic demands and selective pressures on each sex. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches a reported maximum of 1,200,000 grams [Wwi = 1,200,000 grams], or approximately 1,200 kilograms. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight for males is substantially greater, with accounts of 2,200,000 grams [Wwi = 2,200,000 grams], representing a nearly twofold increase in body mass compared to females. This divergence in mass is accompanied by a corresponding difference in linear dimensions; the ultimate total length for a female false killer whale typically reaches about 510 centimeters [Li = about 510 centimeters], whereas males can achieve an ultimate total length of up to 610 centimeters [Li = up to 610 centimeters]. Such pronounced sexual size dimorphism is characteristic of species with intense male-male competition and suggests that larger body size confers a significant advantage in male reproductive success.

The species exhibits an extended lifespan and a slow, K-selected life history strategy, consistent with its role as a large apex predator. The maximum lifespan for false killer whales has been reliably estimated at approximately 62.5 years [am = approximately 62.5 years], a value determined through long-term photographic identification and mark-recapture studies of known individuals under the thermal regime typical of this warm-bodied mammal at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. Consistent with this protracted lifespan, the maximum annual reproductive rate is remarkably low. Observations indicate that a female produces, on average, one calf per reproductive event [N_R_i = one calf per reproductive event], and the interbirth interval yields approximately 0.1 reproductive events per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.1 reproductive events per year] when measured at the species' core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. Such an exceedingly slow reproductive output, combined with a long generation time and extended parental care, renders the species highly vulnerable to population declines from anthropogenic threats such as fisheries bycatch and noise pollution.
